title: Pour One Out for the Leap Second
gist: BIPM will stop issuing leap seconds in May 2027, ending a decades-long practice that has caused failures in UTC-dependent systems like Qantas's booking system. The move was hastened by the rising odds of a never-tested negative leap second as climate change speeds up Earth's rotation; a far-off leap hour will replace it.

themes.theme: BIPM abolishes the leap second from May 2027

insights.claim: The International Bureau of Weights and Measures (BIPM) said it will stop issuing leap seconds in May 2027, after 32 have been added to UTC since 1972.
insights.speaker: Brian Kahn
insights.so_what: Removes a recurring, known failure mode for UTC-dependent infrastructure, APIs and databases.

insights.claim: Leap seconds exist because Earth's rotation, used for astronomical time UT1, is slowing mainly due to tidal friction from the moon, creating drift versus atomic-clock UTC.
insights.speaker: Brian Kahn
insights.so_what: Explains why time drift is structural and will persist even after leap seconds end.

insights.claim: Instead of a leap second, BIPM agreed to create a leap hour, which is millennia away; systems relying on UT1 will need to handle a UT1-UTC offset that grows beyond 1 second.
insights.speaker: Brian Kahn
insights.so_what: Software using astronomical time (e.g., navigation/astronomy systems) faces a new requirement to handle larger UT1-UTC offsets.
